title: Electronic-Entropy-Driven Phase Transitions in Compressed Iron Oxides
authors: S. Azadi, S. M. Vinko, C. Crepisson, A. Principi, T. D. Kuehne, M. S. Bahramy
abstract: Electronic entropy is usually treated as a secondary correction to structural stability, but under strong electronic excitation it can become a primary thermodynamic driving force. Here we show that electronic entropy can drive both polymorphic and stoichiometric phase transformations in compressed iron oxides. Using finite-temperature density functional theory, we calculate the electronic-temperature-dependent Gibbs free energies of Fe$_2$O, FeO, Fe$_4$O$_5$, Fe$_3$O$_4$, and multiple Fe$_2$O$_3$ polymorphs, including $α$-, $ι$-, $ζ$-, $η$-, and $θ$-Fe$_2$O$_3$, over the pressure range 60--260 GPa. At 60-140 GPa, electronic excitation mainly reorganizes the relative stability of Fe$_2$O$_3$ polymorphs, driving transitions from $ι$-Fe$_2$O$_3$ to $η$-Fe$_2$O$_3$. At 180 GPa, the free-energy landscape becomes strongly competitive as FeO is stabilized over an intermediate range of electronic temperature, while $η$-Fe$_2$O$_3$ becomes favourable at higher T. At 220-260 GPa, the lowest-free-energy phase at low T is the Fe-rich compound Fe$_2$O, but increasing electronic temperature stabilizes FeO. These results demonstrate that electronic entropy can control not only the relative stability of crystal structures at fixed composition, but also the competition between different iron-oxide stoichiometries. The predicted electronic-entropy-driven phase boundaries provide a route to nonthermal structural transformations in ultrafast and high-energy-density experiments.
summary: This theoretical work uses finite-temperature DFT to show that electronic entropy is a major thermodynamic driver for phase changes in compressed iron oxides. By calculating the Gibbs free energy across varying pressures and electronic temperatures, the authors map out phase boundaries that govern transitions between different crystal structures and stoichiometries. This work provides a computational route to predict non-thermal structural transformations relevant to high-energy-density experiments.
main_problem: The study investigates how electronic entropy can act as a primary thermodynamic driving force, controlling both polymorphic and stoichiometric phase transformations in compressed iron oxides.

method: The authors employ finite-temperature density functional theory (FT-DFT) to calculate the electronic-temperature-dependent Gibbs free energies of various iron oxide polymorphs.
model_or_system: The system under study is a set of iron oxides ($	ext{Fe}_x	ext{O}_y$), including multiple polymorphs of $	ext{Fe}_2	ext{O}_3$, compressed across pressures up to 260 GPa. The calculations model the system in a two-temperature regime where electronic excitation is significant.

important_parameters: Pressure range of 60–260 GPa and electronic temperature ($T$) up to several eV.

paper_structure: The paper systematically calculates and compares the Gibbs free energies of multiple iron oxide polymorphs across varying pressures and electronic temperatures, identifying the phase boundaries where electronic entropy drives transitions.
why_interesting: The explicit inclusion of electronic entropy as a primary thermodynamic variable provides a framework for understanding non-equilibrium phase transitions in extreme matter, which is relevant to understanding energy deposition and material stability in high-energy physics contexts.
